title: This Too Is for the Good
summary: Nachum Ish Gamzu sets out to bring the emperor a chest full of precious jewels, but in the night someone swaps them for dirt. "This too is for the good," says Nachum, and keeps going. At the palace it turns out that this dirt is a true wonder. A funny story about optimism, and about waiting a moment before deciding that something is bad.
pages: Once there was a wise man named Nachum. He was a happy, calm man, and no matter what happened to him, he always said: "This too is for the good." Spilled his soup? "This too is for the good." It started to rain? "This too is for the good." That's why everyone called him "Nachum Ish Gamzu", Nachum the This-Too man.

One day the sages of Israel wanted to send a gift to the emperor, the great king of Rome. "Who will bring the gift?" they asked. "Nachum," they decided. "Miracles happen to him." They gave him a chest full of precious stones and pearls, sparkling and beautiful.

Nachum set out on the long road. In the evening he came to an inn, a little hotel for travelers, and asked to sleep there. He put the chest beside his bed and fell asleep. But in the night, while Nachum slept, the people of the inn quietly opened the chest, took all the precious stones, and filled it up with... dirt.

In the morning Nachum got up, opened the chest, and saw: dirt. Only dry brown dirt. What would you have said? Nachum looked, took a deep breath, and said: "This too is for the good." He closed the chest and went on his way.

When he reached the palace, Nachum handed the chest to the emperor. The emperor opened it and saw dirt. His face turned red with anger. "The Jews are making fun of me!" he shouted. "They send me dirt as a gift?" And the ministers all around him grumbled too.

Then a man who looked like one of the ministers stepped up to the emperor. But he was not just any minister: he was Elijah the Prophet, who had come to help. "Wait," he said. "Maybe this is the dirt of our father Abraham? They say that when Abraham threw dirt, it turned into swords, and straw turned into arrows, and that is how he defeated his enemies."

In those days there was one city the emperor had not been able to conquer for a very long time. "Let's try it," he said. They took some of the dirt and sent it there, and a wonder happened: thanks to the dirt, the emperor's army won, and the city was taken. The emperor could hardly believe it. "What a marvelous gift!"

The emperor was so happy that he filled Nachum's chest with precious stones and pearls and sent him home with great honor. "This too is for the good," Nachum smiled. And this time everyone understood why.

On the way back, Nachum passed by the same inn again. The innkeepers were amazed to see him so honored. "What did you bring the emperor?" they asked.
"What I took from here, I brought there," Nachum answered simply.

"Aha!" thought the innkeepers. "Our dirt is worth a treasure!" They filled big sacks with dirt from the yard and dragged them all the way to the emperor. But their dirt was just plain dirt, and no wonder happened at all. They went home tired, disappointed and empty-handed.

"This too is for the good" doesn't mean that everything is always nice. It means waiting a moment before deciding that something is bad. Ran out of blue paint? Maybe you'll discover there's a purple moon in the world. Rain on the day of the trip? Maybe you'll find the perfect puddle for jumping. Try saying "This too is for the good" sometime, and see what happens.
